subject: Career
title: Framing: How You Present the Ask
description: A 60-second lesson on Framing: How You Present the Ask.

hook.text: 'I need more money' vs. 'Based on my impact and the market, here's what's fair.' Same ask, different frame.

buildup.text: Framing changes how the same information is received. Needs-based asks feel desperate.

discovery.text: Value-based framing positions you as a partner: 'Here's what I bring and what that's worth.'

twist.text: Even the word choice matters. 'I'd like' is weaker than 'I'm looking for' which is weaker than 'I'm targeting.'

climax.text: Frame the negotiation as collaborative: 'How do we close this gap together?'

punchline.text: Same number, different frame, different outcome.

quiz.question: Which framing is most effective in salary negotiation?
options: Value-based: 'Here's what I bring and what it's worth'
Needs-based: 'I need more to pay rent'
Emotional: 'I'll be upset if you don't'

details.summary: Framing your salary request around the value you deliver rather than personal need changes how the employer evaluates it. Positioning a raise as an investment in retention and productivity makes the conversation collaborative rather than adversarial.
details.whyItMatters: Employers evaluate compensation in terms of return on investment. Framing your ask as value-aligned rather than need-based increases the probability of approval.
takeaways: Frame raises as investments, not personal expense requests
Quantify your contributions before any compensation talk
Collaborative framing reduces defensiveness on both sides

faq.question: What is an example of value-based framing for a raise?
faq.answer: Instead of saying 'I need a raise because of my expenses,' say 'My work on Project X generated $200,000 in new revenue this quarter, and I would like my compensation to reflect that contribution.' This positions you as presenting a business case.

faq.question: Is it ever appropriate to mention personal financial needs?
faq.answer: Personal circumstances are generally not persuasive in corporate settings. Employers set pay based on market rate and value delivered. However, in small teams with close relationships, mentioning relocation costs or life changes can add human context.
